summary:
Tyumen Oblast is a region of Russia, and the Russian national framework applies in full across its territory. Since 2022 the national regime has tightened sharply: Putin signed the law banning gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents in 2023, the Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and the expanded propaganda law criminalises any public expression, including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and national government warnings explicitly advise LGBT travellers of this risk. The US State Department lists Russia at Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

The UK Home Office country policy information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025, assessment section updated 11 June 2025) sets the conditions in force in Tyumen Oblast. It records that same-sex activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and no discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation or gender identity covers housing, healthcare or employment. The note records no region-specific findings: it states the national conditions that operate across all of Russia, this region included.

Penalties under the national framework are severe. 'Gay propaganda' offences carry fines up to 400,000 roubles (about £3,600) for individuals or up to 15 days' detention, and repeat offences can bring criminal prosecution with up to four years in prison. The November 2023 Supreme Court extremist designation of the international LGBT+ movement makes participation punishable by two to six years and organising by six to ten years.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions tied to the International Public LGBT Movement designation, approximately 98 administrative and three criminal. The Supreme Court ruling entered into force in January 2024 and opened the way to arbitrary prosecutions of LGBT people and their supporters. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation: two were sentenced to prison and one died by suicide in pretrial detention. A further 81 people in 98 court cases were found guilty of administrative offences for displaying banned symbols, with fines up to 2,000 roubles, and repeat displays are punishable under the criminal code by up to four years in prison.

On 15 May 2025 investigators charged three publishing-house staff under article 282.2 for selling fiction exploring LGBT themes, an offence carrying up to 12 years. Between December 2022 and March 2024 at least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws, and the Home Office assesses that trans people, publicly active LGBT+ advocates and those in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement has grown in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million roubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk in Siberia, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tyumen Oblast live under the same national prohibitions as visitors, with no regional protection layer. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been unavailable since 2023, and no discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation or gender identity covers housing, healthcare or employment, so complaints about denial of service, dismissal or housing refusal have no statutory basis.

Everyday conduct carries administrative and criminal exposure. Displaying symbols of the designated movement has produced 81 convictions across 98 court cases with fines up to 2,000 roubles, and a repeat display is charged under the criminal code at up to four years. Participation in the designated organisation is punishable by two to six years and organising by six to ten. At least 139 people were affected by anti-LGBT+ enforcement between December 2022 and March 2024.

For residents seeking protection abroad, the UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, and assesses trans people and publicly active LGBT+ advocates as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. That standard governs UK asylum claims.
outOfScopeNotes:
The UK Home Office note records no region-specific findings for Tyumen Oblast. No Tyumen-specific prosecutions, raids, local ordinances or incidents are sourced in the underlying material, so conditions stated for this region are drawn from the national framework and from nationally aggregated enforcement data rather than from local evidence.

The enforcement counts carry fixed cut-off dates: the Human Rights Watch figures run to 30 June 2025 and the Home Office affected-persons count covers December 2022 to March 2024. Whether subsequent cases have been brought in Tyumen Oblast is unresolved on the sources available.

The rouble-to-pound and rouble-to-dollar conversions are approximate and move with the exchange rate. Whether any Tyumen Oblast authority has issued directives on public assembly, venue licensing or documentation beyond the federal statutes is not sourced here.
